10337-lady-into-fox:
David Garnett published this strange novella in 1922, with wood engravings by R. A. Garnett. Its premise is plain and startling: Mrs. Tebrick suddenly changes into a vixen, a fact proved, the narrator says, by a dozen respectable witnesses. The tale then asks what a husband does when his wife becomes a fox.

Garnett tells the event with calm, exact prose, refusing to explain the marvel away. Love, duty, and wild nature pull Mr. Tebrick in opposite ways. Readers get a witty, haunting fable about marriage, change, and the animal life that lurks beneath civil manners.
14863-the-tinder-box:
Maria Thompson Daviess's 1913 novel is dedicated to Hannah Daviess Pittman, who blazed her trail. It takes its title from fire: a load, a maiden lance, a flint spark, and the question whether love is sweeter when tamed. Deeper than shoulders or ribs, a man and an asafoetida spoon, and some smoulderings follow.

An attained tomorrow, dynamite and the closing question together close the chapters. Daviess, author of The Melting of Molly and Miss Selina Lue, writes a Southern romance of strong feeling and sharp talk, illustrated by John Edwin Jackson. The tinder box stands for a temper that catches quickly, and a love that may burn or warm a household.
1585-the-wrong-box:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Lloyd Osbourne's farce follows the Finsbury family, whose members await a tontine fortune payable to the last survivor. Morris Finsbury suspects his brother, a wrong box is shipped, and a comedy of corpses, trains, and mistaken bodies runs riot through London.

The preface pleads judicious levity, and the book delivers it: black humour, brisk plotting, and a cast of rogues and innocents. Stevenson and Osbourne enjoy the macabre game. The Wrong Box is a classic Victorian farce, dark, funny, and perfect for readers who like their crime played for laughs.
16681-baby-chatterbox:
R. Worthington's 1880 Baby Chatterbox gathers verses and pictures for the very young. The New Baby opens the book. A soft baby with violet eyes comes down from the sky in the night, carried by angels from the far-away blue, a present to reader and child. Dolly's Promenade follows, urging a lazy dolly to walk and talk.

The verses are short, sweet, and made for reading aloud to small children. Pictures lighten every page. As a period piece, the book shows Victorian nursery verse at its gentlest, full of angels, dolls, and loving talk.
17197-the-black-box:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1915 Black Box, in its photoplay edition, stars Sanford Quest, criminologist, played on screen by Herbert Rawlinson. Chapters follow an apartment-house mystery, hidden hands, a pocket wireless, an old grudge, the rack, an unseen terror, and a house of mystery. Lost in London, a ship of horror, a desert vengeance, and tongues of flame push the plot on.

Pictures from the Universal film, with Lenora MacDougal played by Anna Little, match the text scene by scene. Oppenheim writes in his smooth, popular thriller style, with science, crime, and chase in turn. Mystery fans will enjoy a fast, visual novel from the early age of film tie-ins.
17677-the-tree-of-appomattox:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote this story of the Civil War's close, first published in 1916 by D. Appleton and Company, in a series that also includes The Guns of Bull Run, The Guns of Shiloh, and The Star of Gettysburg. Chapters open with the apple tree and the woman at the house. Over the hills, a fight at the crossways, and an old enemy follow.

The fishermen, Sheridan's attack, and a messenger from Richmond carry the tale toward Appomattox. A grip with Early and an unbeaten foe close the set. Readers get a boys' Civil War novel of the war's last campaigns, brisk and patriotic. Altsheler's series suits young readers of American history fiction.
18140-an-alabaster-box:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman and Florence Morse Kingsley wrote An Alabaster Box in 1917, printed in New York and London by D. Appleton, with pictures by Stockton Mulford. The title quotes the woman who broke a box of precious ointment, and the tale takes its tone from that act of costly love.

The book opens with Mrs. Solomon Black vowing to raise the minister's salary by a church fair, though Wesley Elliot calls fairs sheer beggary. She answers, then we will beg. Freeman and Kingsley write with dry humor and New England warmth. It is a gentle, old tale of a church, a town, and the price of giving.
1825-the-adventures-of-reddy-fox:
Thornton W. Burgess tells of Reddy Fox, a young fox sent to live with Granny Fox because his mother has too many hungry mouths to feed. Granny, the wisest and slyest fox in the country round, takes Reddy hunting each day . She teaches him what every fox should know: how to steal a meal, how to dodge a dog, and how to read the signs of the Green Forest.

The chapters follow Reddy's lessons and his scrapes with Peter Rabbit, Johnny Chuck, and the other small folk of the meadow. Written for children, the book mixes animal adventure with plain advice about care and caution, and it remains a gentle introduction to Burgess's whole world of woodland neighbors.
18667-doctor-rabbit-and-brushtail-the-fo:
Thomas Clark Hinkle wrote this Greenwood Series tale, published by Rand McNally at Chicago and New York, pictures by Milo Winter. It opens in the Big Green Woods, where Doctor Rabbit and Cheepy Chipmunk sit talking on a fine morning. A reddish-brown beast with a big bushy tail appears under the trees, and Cheepy knows at once the newcomer spells danger for rabbits, chipmunks, and friends.

Chapters follow Brushtail the fox playing possum, getting a scare, stealing a hen, finding cheese, and dodging traps laid by Doctor Rabbit. Two hunters, a sprained foot, a doctored woodchuck, and an exciting chase fill later pages. The book is a gentle woodland adventure for young readers.
20208-boy-scouts-in-the-philippines-or-t:
Boy Scouts in the Philippines, from 1911, sends its troop across the Pacific. Frank means to sleep again aboard ship but fails at once. Jimmie grabs him by the shoulders and dumps him on a scarlet rug. The rug covers the floor of their shared stateroom at sea.

Horseplay soon gives way to the key to the treaty box. That object drives the plot once the boys reach the islands. Scout tales of this era mix travel, teamwork, and patriotic missions. Readers get a lively trip to the Philippines as Americans then pictured it.
22106-john-knox:
John Knox, the thundering preacher who remade Scotland's church, is the subject of this biography. Knox spent years in exile and in a French galley before his hour came. The writer compares him to the old prophets who waited in the desert. Like them, Knox was hidden until the day of his showing to his people.

The life follows his preaching, his clashes with Mary Queen of Scots, and the building of the Reformed Kirk. Knox's rough spear-head manner gets full credit for breaking Rome's hold on Scotland. This account treats him as a hero of faith and nation. It shows the place Knox still held in Protestant memory centuries after his death.
2344-the-adventure-of-the-cardboard-box:
Sherlock Holmes investigates a gruesome parcel in The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, in which a woman receives two severed ears by post. Arthur Conan Doyle builds the case from small clues: the knots, the address, and a tragic triangle of love and revenge. Holmes reads the package like a book, and Watson watches in horror and admiration.

The story's solution turns on jealousy and a sailor's secret past, with a sadness beneath the sensation. It ranks among the darker Holmes shorts. Mystery fans will find a compact, chilling case.
28509-the-brass-bound-box:
Evelyn Raymond's The Brass Bound Box, copyrighted in 1905, is set in Marsden, a village still remote from any railway line. Its chief events are the morning and evening arrivals of the mail-coach, whose driver Reuben Smith blows a horn as he approaches the general store and post-office.

Into this quiet place comes a legacy, and a legatee named Montgomery Sturtevant, called Monty, whose story unfolds through foxes' gully, chestnuts, gold mines, and the brass-bound box of chapter six. Squire Pettijohn, Alf, and other villagers fill out a tale of village life, mystery, and neighbourly help. Raymond writes warmly for young readers.
28705-the-god-in-the-box:
Sewell Peaslee Wright's The God in the Box, from Astounding Stories of September 1931, is Commander John Hanson's tale. Hanson says he never meant to tell it, but Zenian friends fret him with boasts that Ame Baove, a Zenian, first mastered space. Baove's log is a school classic, yet Hanson commanded the Ertak through her whole active life and holds another story.

On routine Special Patrol duty, orders send the Ertak to inspect an unvisited planet passing near their line, contacting its people if inhabited, which was doubted. Hanson, then a youngster of half a century, resolves a unique and poignant mystery. Readers get space adventure told as an old officer's answer to a boast.
29005-prince-vance-the-story-of-a-prince:
Eleanor Putnam and Arlo Bates wrote this 1888 children's fantasy, Prince Vance: The Story of a Prince with a Court in His Box. Roberts Brothers in Boston published it, with pictures by Frank Myrick. The book is dedicated to the boy Oric, in verses about a twisted, tangled web of whims woven while he scarcely knew speech. The story follows a prince whose whole court fits in a box.

Pictures show the fairy Copetta and the prince, a tutor set laughing on a window sill, and a blue wizard holding out a gold bonbon box. The royal table shrinks its court, and a king takes a bath in a finger bowl. Readers get a whimsical Victorian fantasy for children, playful and tender, written by a mother and a poet for a small boy.
29757-the-story-of-a-tinder-box:
Charles Meymott Tidy gave these talks to young listeners in London during the Christmas holidays of 1888-89, and they were printed in 1897. He starts from the plain tinder-box, the small kit once used to catch a spark and coax it into flame. From there he works through the tools and tricks that came after it. The tone stays plain and homely, as befits talks meant for a holiday crowd rather than for trained chemists.

Tidy links each device to the fire it made and the daily life it served, from striking flint on steel to the early match. Short trials and homely examples carry the science, so a young reader can follow how a spark became a steady flame. The lectures keep their spoken feel, with thanks to firms that lent gear for the live trials.
29852-the-ivory-snuff-box:
Arnold Fredericks published The Ivory Snuff Box in New York in 1912, with Grosset and Dunlap. Richard Duvall, a detective, leaves the office of Monsieur Lefevre, Prefect of Police of Paris, with fateful words in his ears: the fortunes of a nation may depend upon your faithfulness. Vernet, one of the Prefect's assistants, rides with him through the torrent of traffic on the Rue de Rivoli.

Duvall's thoughts run to Grace, his wife, Grace Ellicott until little more than an hour before. He had hoped to be bound for Cherbourg and New York with her, on a shipboard honeymoon. Instead he heads for London on a mysterious expedition, while Grace waits for him in vain at the pension. Fredericks builds a brisk spy tale from a wedding day broken by duty.
31021-the-bandbox:
Louis Joseph Vance, author of The Brass Bowl, The Bronze Bell, and Cynthia-of-the-Minute, wrote this adventure novel, published by A. L. Burt in New York in April 1912, with four pictures by Arthur I. Keller and copyright in 1911 and 1912. It is dedicated to Lewis Buddy III. Its seventeen chapters run from Introducing Mr. Iff and The Bandbox through Twins, Queenstown, Ismay, Iff, Stole Away, and The Wrong Box.

Later chapters bring A Likely Story, Dead o' Night, The Cold Grey Dawn, Won't You Walk into My Parlour, Wreck Island, The Strong-Box, The Enemy's Hand, Ninety Minutes, and Holocaust. The book opens at half-past two of a sunny, warm, sultry afternoon late in August, and its frontispiece shows a woman exclaiming, Now, sir, as she turns. It is a fast, twist-filled tale built around a bandbox and the people who want it.
32537-the-newsboy-partners-or-who-was-di:
Frank V. Webster's The Newsboy Partners, copyrighted in 1909, follows Jimmy Small, a newsboy shouting extras in City Hall Park, New York. Jimmy sells papers about a great fire, outshouting a dozen ragged rivals as customers rush past, and his luck soon turns when he meets a strange boy who becomes Dick Box.

Chapters follow a box for a bed, a new name, nursing, lessons in letters, a newsboy partnership, and threats from Bulldog and Conroy. The story ends by revealing who Dick Box was, turning a street tale of pennies, stands, and loyalty into a mystery about a lost boy's true name.
33941-the-methods-of-glass-blowing-and-o:
W. A. Shenstone, formerly a lecturer in chemistry at Clifton College, wrote this manual of glass blowing, in a ninth impression published in London in 1916. It serves chemical and physical students who must shape glass and work silica in the oxy-gas flame. Chapters open with the glass-blower's apparatus, workplace, blow-pipe, and bellows.

Later chapters cover varieties of glass, joints, seals, and the handling of silica. Shenstone writes for the bench, with steps a student can follow. The manual remains a useful record of laboratory craft before ready-made glassware took over.
3767-the-man-who-kept-his-money-in-a-box:
Anthony Trollope tells this comic travel tale through a narrator named Robinson, who meets the man of the title in the gorge of the Via Mala. The stranger, called Greene for the story, crosses Switzerland and Italy with his wife, guarding a box of money as if it were a child. At the Splugen hospice, at Chiavenna, and at Bellaggio on Lake Como, his caution grows more comic at each halt.

Mrs Greene adds to the fun by playing the grand lady at Bellaggio, ordering about waiters with a manner her husband finds hard to bear. The tale pokes gentle fun at English travelers, their cash, and their pride. Readers who enjoy Trollope in a light mood will find a short story that turns a holiday worry into a neat study of vanity.
4039-volpone-or-the-fox:
Ben Jonson's comedy follows Volpone, a rich Venetian who feigns sickness to draw gifts from men hoping to be his heir. His servant Mosca helps stage the fraud, flattering each suitor with tales of a suffering, wise, grave master whose every word is worth a gold coin.

A loud knock breaks the game, and the plot spins through greed, lust, and law in Jonson's sharpest manner. The play's beasts in human dress, fox, fly, and vulture, give it its bite. Readers who enjoy fierce, funny satire will find Volpone a fast, crowded comedy about money and the people who chase it.
4980-old-granny-fox:
Thornton W. Burgess's Old Granny Fox follows Reddy Fox and his grandmother through hunting, dreams, and old age in the Green Forest. Reddy brings Granny news, doubts her senses, fears to go home, and grows impudent, while Quacker the Duck grows curious and Farmer Brown's boy shapes the story's dangers.

Granny is caught napping, has a bad dream, admits growing old, and makes three vain and foolish wishes, yet Reddy is made truly happy in the end. Burgess mixes animal comedy with gentle lessons about age and family. Young readers get a woodland tale where a grandmother's wisdom, even when doubted, proves its worth.
5610-the-cardinal-s-snuff-box:
Henry Harland wrote The Cardinal's Snuff-Box as a romance set in Italy, opening with a small, perfect scene. Old Marietta asks the Signorino whether he will take coffee, setting fruit before him. Peter deliberates, then decides: yes, but in the garden, certainly, not perhaps. The little brown old woman's sharp black Italian eyes twinkle as she promises a rustic table under the big willow at the water's edge.

The novel follows Peter among Italian gardens, villas, and society, with a cardinal's snuff-box at its center as a token of favor and mystery. Harland writes with lightness and color. Readers get an Edwardian Italian romance, charming, witty, and full of sunlit detail.
5639-the-progressive-democracy-of-james-:
Charles E. Morris, secretary to Governor Cox, wrote The Progressive Democracy of James M. Cox as a portrait of a doer for a postwar age. Morris opens with a call for not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work. A great and devastating war has ended, its moral lesson taught and learned in penitence, yet victory's fruits stay ungathered and peace's beneficence unattained.

Two great American parties, both with splendid accomplishments, face that moment, and Cox stands as the progressive answer. Readers get a campaign-era political book, earnest and partisan, about leadership after the First World War.
5955-the-tale-of-tommy-fox:
The Tale of Tommy Fox follows a young fox learning to hunt, in chapters from Tommy enjoying himself through Johnnie Green going hunting. Tommy learns to hunt, meets Mother Grouse's children, grows hungry, mistakes Mr Gray Squirrel, chases Mr Woodchuck, and grows very proud, before trouble comes and Mrs Fox outwits Dog Spot. One hunt shows Tommy leaping for old Mother Grouse, missing as she rises in the nick of time.

She flies a little further, lights, and seems to forget Tommy is near, and the same escape repeats again and again to his annoyance. Young readers learn woodland hunting through comedy, where prey outwits predator by timing and luck. The book suits early readers and bedtime stories, with short chapters, animal neighbors, and a fox hero whose pride meets its match in grouse and dogs.
6578-the-man-on-the-box:
Harold MacGrath builds his comedy on a mix-up: a hero who takes a groom's place, a heroine who hires him, and a house full of plots. The chapters promise a family reunion, a police affair, a first ride, a runaway, and a stove pipe episode, all leading to a castle of romance. The book grew from a stage hit that ran 123 nights in New York.

Love, bluff, and social climbing drive the fun, as the man on the box must play his part without giving himself away. MacGrath keeps the scenes brisk and the talk light, with each new scrape worse than the last. The Man on the Box is a gay, old-style farce of mistaken rank and true feeling.
an-alabaster-box: Mary Eleanor Wilkins Freeman writes An Alabaster Box, a novel of New England life told across short chapters of domestic and moral drama. The story follows its heroine through family duty, love, and conscience in a small town world. Freeman's plain, exact prose gives the book its force, and its place among her studies of village character.
baby-chatterbox:
An anonymous picture book for the nursery, copyrighted by R. Worthington of New York in 1880, this volume mixes verse and short tales for very small children. The New Baby opens it, a poem about a soft baby with violet eyes. She came down from the sky in the night. Angels carried her from the arms of God, a present to the household. Kiss her and love her, the poem instructs.

Stories follow in large, gentle type. Faithful Tray hears the baby crying alone, runs upstairs, and fetches nurse to the rescue. My Friend Washington begins another childhood memoir in simple sentences. Transcribers corrected the battered print word by word, could'nt to couldn't and foxglore to foxglove. A battered survivor of the Victorian nursery shelf remains, all morals, animals, and baby talk.
britannica-1911-chicken-pox:
Chicken-pox, also called varicella, is a specific contagious disease marked by an eruption of vesicles in the skin. It usually comes in epidemics and belongs to childhood, with patients generally between two and six years old. The incubation period runs from ten to fifteen days, and there are almost no warning symptoms. A slight fever for about a day comes first, and then the eruption makes its appearance on the trunk.

Raised red papules turn within a day into tense vesicles of clear fluid, which then grows cloudy and dries by the fourth day. Fresh spots appear over the first three days, so spots in all stages can be seen at once. The course is usually mild, scars are rare, and one attack does not give immunity. Five points for telling the disease from smallpox close the entry, covering spread, shape, speed and depth of the spots.
britannica-1911-fox:
Fox, the female being the vixen, is properly the name of the single wild British member of the dog family, the Canidae. In a wider sense it denotes fox-like species from all parts of the world. Many South American kinds carry the name though they do not truly belong to the same group. Linnaeus placed the fox in one genus with the dog and the wolf, as Canis vulpes. Most naturalists now make it the type of a genus of its own, Vulpes, as Vulpes alopex or Vulpes vulpes.

Foxes are told from dogs, wolves and jackals by a mark in the skull. The projection behind the eye socket is concave on its upper surface, with a raised ridge in front, where in Canis it is evenly convex. The long article treats the fox's body, habits, hunting and kinds across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-antoi:
Charles-Antoine Coysevox was a French sculptor born at Lyons in 1640 and dead at Paris in 1720, from a family of Spanish origin. At seventeen he carved a much admired Madonna, and in 1671 Louis XIV employed him on sculptures at Versailles and Marly. Elected to the Academy in 1676, he taught his nephews Nicolas and Guillaume Coustou. He made two bronze statues of Louis XIV and a Charlemagne for Saint-Louis des Invalides. His best known work is probably La Renommée at the Tuileries entrance: two winged horses carrying Mercury and Fame.

The emperor Napoleon is said to have loved the sculptor's fancy that Mercury's horse wears a bridle while Fame's has none. Coysevox also carved fine tombs for Paris churches, and his contemporary portraits earn him a special debt from later ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-knox:
John Knox was the Scottish Protestant leader whose History of the Reformation shaped his country's story. Born at Haddington between 1505 and 1515 to a probably small farming family, he was schooled there. He knew Latin and French, some Greek and Hebrew, and law. He was ordained a priest and practiced as a notary by apostolic authority. Nothing is known of his early church career, and by 1540 he was tutoring children.

His own History, written some eighteen years after the events, first brings him into view in 1545. He appears as devoted disciple of George Wishart, the Protestant preacher then intriguing with Henry VIII against Cardinal Beaton. From that discipleship Knox rose to become Scotland's most prominent exponent of the new doctrines. He was a preacher of formidable vernacular power whose movement overthrew the old Church and fixed the Reformed faith in Scotland before his death at Edinburgh in 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-robert-wi:
Robert Wilcox was an English martyr born at Chester in 1558, who suffered at Canterbury on 1 October 1588. He reached Reims on 12 August 1583 and received tonsure and minor orders on 23 September following. Ordained subdeacon in March, deacon in April, and priest on 20 April 1585, all at Reims, he was sent on the mission on 7 January 1586. He was jailed in the Marshalsea that same year.

Two other priests, Christopher Buxton and Edward Campion, suffered with him, along with the layman Robert Widmerpool. Edward Campion, truly Edwards, was born in 1552 at Ludlow in Shropshire of a good family. He was schooled two years at Jesus College, Oxford, and afterwards served Gregory, tenth Lord Dacre of the South. He reached Reims on 22 February 1586, took the name Campion, and was ordained subdeacon, deacon, and priest there before his mission and execution.
lady-into-fox:
David Garnett published Lady into Fox in October 1922. Wood engravings by R. A. Garnett illustrate it. Garnett opens by noting that marvels come in uneven crops across the centuries.

His marvel is simple and strange: Mrs. Tebrick turns into a fox. Her husband must face life with a wife who is now an animal. Garnett tells the change in calm, plain prose. That calm makes each new loss feel sharper. The short novel became a quiet classic of English fantasy. The wood engravings add a storybook feel to a sad tale. Garnett keeps the ending quiet rather than spectacular.
longstreet-manassas-appomattox:
James Longstreet, Lee's senior corps commander, published From Manassas to Appomattox in 1896. Southern critics had blamed Longstreet for the loss at Gettysburg, and he wrote to defend himself. Lee had called him his Old War Horse.

Longstreet narrates the eastern war from First Manassas to the surrender, with maps and frank judgments. He defends his moves at Gettysburg and faults others, including Lee's plan there. His friendship with Grant, his old army comrade, colors the closing chapters. The memoir is key, and contested, evidence on how the Confederacy lost its greatest battles. Maps and returns from his own files back many of his claims.
nasa-tm-19670030753-a-resonance-tube-ign:
E. William Conrad and Albert J. Pavli, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, report a flameless lighter for rockets in this October 1967 memorandum. The device is a resonance-tube igniter for hydrogen-oxygen engines. A resonance tube heats gas at its closed end through pressure waves alone, with no spark.

The authors studied the resonance effects and tuned them using a burning mixture ratio of hydrogen and oxygen. Their data show how the tube's geometry changes the temperature reached at the cavity bottom. That peak heat proved enough to ignite the mixture. The test demonstrated that a resonance tube can serve as an igniter.
nasa-tm-19720024159-apollo-16-mission-an:
Apollo 16 flew in 1972, and this report deals with a failure found after the mission. The Mission Evaluation Team at Houston prepared it in June 1972. Owen G. Morris, manager of the Apollo Spacecraft Program, approved it. Its subject is a tank used while draining oxidizer from the command module.

Ground crews emptied leftover propellant from the reaction control system after flight. Their gear was built to make the propellant safe, in both liquid and gas form, before disposal. The report records what went wrong with the oxidizer tank during that work. Such reports helped NASA fix faults before later flights.
old-granny-fox:
Thornton Waldo Burgess wrote this animal story for children. Granny Fox and Reddy Fox hunt through a hard winter. Snow covers the meadows, and ice binds the pool. Food is scarce, so they hunt almost all day. Farmer Brown's boy and Bowser the Hound threaten them.

The contents list traps, storms, and a midnight hen hunt. Granny admits she is growing old and slower. Reddy learns respect for her wisdom and skill. Burgess teaches nature lore through each small adventure. Gentle morals close the tales of the Green Forest. Winter hunger makes each small choice matter for the foxes' survival.
reynard-the-fox: John Masefield's Reynard the Fox appears here in a new edition from Macmillan of New York, dated 1920. Copyrights of 1919 and 1920 stand on its pages. Eight plates in colour and many other pictures, by Carton Moorepark, adorn the edition. The opening pages shown are its title and copyright pages only. They give the poet's name, the painter's, and the edition's dates. No verse of the poem itself is printed in the pages at hand.
the-adventure-of-the-cardboard-box:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventure of the Cardboard Box as a Sherlock Holmes tale, told by Dr. Watson. Watson opens with a short plea about his choice of cases, saying he picks tales that show Holmes's mind at work with as little cheap thrill as he can.

He grants that crime and shock cannot be split clean, so some grim matter must stand. The scene then shifts to a blazing hot day in August, with Baker Street like an oven and sun glare on the bricks across the road. Holmes lies curled on the sofa, reading a fresh letter over and over. Readers get one of the darkest Holmes tales, sparked by a plain box in the post.
the-adventures-of-reddy-fox:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Reddy Fox, first of his Green Forest tales for children. Chapter one, Granny Fox Gives Reddy a Scare, sets the pair at home on the Green Meadows' edge.

Reddy, one of a large litter that strained his mother, has been sent to live with old Granny Fox. Burgess calls her the wisest, slyest, smartest fox in all the country round. Each day she takes Reddy hunting and teaches him how to steal Farmer Brown's chickens without waking Bowser the Hound, plus a host of ways to fool a dog. That day she leads him to new ground, the railroad track and a long bridge. Young readers learn woodcraft with the cub.
the-black-box:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's novel, copyrighted in 1915, was issued with pictures taken from a Universal photoplay version. Its hero, shown in a portrait caption, is Sanford Quest, a criminologist. Chapter two names an apartment-house mystery, and chapter three hidden hands.

A pocket wireless, an old grudge, and chapters called On the Rack and The Unseen Terror follow. A house of mystery, an inherited sin, and being lost in London close the opening contents. The tie to a film serial matters here: stills from the screen version illustrate a detective tale built from short, cliff-hanging episodes.
the-cardinal-s-snuff-box:
The Cardinal's Snuff-Box, by Henry Harland, opens with Peter taking coffee in a garden, at old Marietta's insistence, at a rustic table under the big willow at the water's edge. The scene is set before any intrigue: a guest at ease in an Italian garden, pressed to linger over one more cup.

The view does the rest of the introducing. The river Aco runs peacock-green between poplar banks. Across it lies the park of Ventirose with its many-pinnacled castle. The Gnisi and the Cornobastone range stand over it. Monte Sfiorito raises three snow summits through pink vapour. Harland builds the novel's world out of light, water, and mountains before he lets anything happen in it.
the-man-on-the-box: Harold MacGrath wrote The Man on the Box, illustrated with scenes from Walter N. Lawrence's production, which ran 123 nights at the Madison Square Theatre in New York. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the novel does not appear. The chapters promise Introduces My Hero, Introduces My Heroine, The Adventure Begins, and A Family Reunion. The Plot Thickens, the title chapter, A Police Affair, and The Heroine Hires a Groom follow. A chapter called Pirate, The First Ride, and A Runaway close the list.
the-man-who-kept-his-money-in-a-box:
The Man Who Kept His Money in a Box, transcribed from the 1864 Chapman and Hall Tales of All Countries edition, names no author in what is present. Its narrator, addressed as Robinson, first saw his subject in the ravine of the Via Mala in Switzerland. They exchanged words at the hospice atop the Splügen Pass and became acquainted in the courtyard of Conradi's hotel at Chiavenna; the friendship ripened afterward at Bellaggio, on Lake Como.

The man, called Greene for the present, traveled with his wife and daughter. The narrator saw him first through a diligence window in the gorge, nose pressed to the glass, neck twisted painfully upward at the rocks he was too cautious to walk among. A man who keeps his money in a box, met on an Alpine road, gives the tale its quiet comedy of timidity abroad.
the-progressive-democracy-of-james-m-cox:
Charles E. Morris, secretary to Governor Cox, opens The Progressive Democracy of James M. Cox with the need for a doer. A great war has ended, the most devastating in history, but the fruits of victory are ungathered. America, he writes, always produces a man for the great occasion, and its records glow with teachers and doers appearing at the proper time. Two parties with splendid accomplishments and grave mistakes now compete for the hour.

Those who would keep the promises made in France present their leader: James Monroe Cox, Governor of Ohio. The promises include a League of Nations to end war and retribution without blind vengeance. Morris frames the choice as America's high mission to humanity, begun when she threw her power into the war. The book is a campaign-era brief for Cox's progressive democracy.
the-silver-box:
John Galsworthy's play The Silver Box, a comedy in three acts, is introduced in this record by a long modern biography of its author. Galsworthy was born at Kingston upon Thames in 1867, the biography says. He trained as a barrister but found law unattractive. He travelled abroad and befriended Joseph Conrad, then a first mate. His first play was this one, an immediate success at its 1906 debut, the account adds.

The biography stresses his themes of social class and upper-middle class life. It also lists causes he championed, from prison reform to women's rights. A contents list for the play follows the biography. John Barthwick, M.P., heads the persons, with his wife and son Jack. Scenes move between Barthwick's dining-room, the Jones's lodgings, and a London police court. No dialogue of the play itself appears here.
the-tale-of-tommy-fox: Tommy Fox is one of Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales, copyrighted in 1915 and illustrated by Harry L. Smith. A title page and contents list make up this record, leaving Tommy's hunting lessons untold. Twenty-one chapters follow a young fox who learns to hunt, goes hungry, chases Mr. Woodchuck, and is outwitted alongside his mother by Dog Spot. Johnnie Green, the farmer's boy, enters later with a new pet. The headings sketch a cub growing careless, boastful, and finally wiser as winter whitens the world.
the-tinder-box: Maria Thompson Daviess published The Tinder-Box with the Century Company in November 1913, dedicating it to Hannah Daviess Pittman, who blazed her trail. This record shows the illustrated title pages and a contents list, nothing of the novel itself. Ten chapters run from The Load and The Maiden Lance through a flint-spark, smolderings, and dynamite, ending with a chapter titled Together? The fire imagery of the headings promises a suffrage-era romance of a woman finding her spark, but Daviess's heroine speaks only beyond the pages present.
the-tree-of-appomattox: Joseph A. Altsheler's Tree of Appomattox, a story of the Civil War's close, was copyrighted in 1916 by D. Appleton and closes his eight-volume Civil War series. This record gives the copyright page, the series list from The Guns of Bull Run to this final volume, and a cast of principal characters. Harry Kenton fights for the South while his cousin Dick Mason fights for the North, the family division at the series' heart. Altsheler's account of Appomattox itself begins past these pages.
the-wrong-box:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Lloyd Osbourne open The Wrong Box with a teasing preface. They quote their character Michael Finsbury praising judicious levity. One author, they joke, is old enough to be ashamed. The other is young enough to learn better. Chapter one then mocks how readers underrate authors' labors. Research, authorities, and German correspondence all go unnoticed, the narrator complains.

The tale could have begun with a life of Tonti, the narrator says. Tonti invented the tontine, the scheme behind the plot. Instead the scaffolding is knocked down for a comic story. A corpse and a disputed inheritance drive the farce. Readers get Stevenson's lightest, most playful fiction.
volpone-or-the-fox:
Ben Jonson's Volpone, or The Fox, stands here with an introduction that sketches the playwright's life. It calls Jonson the greatest English dramatist after Shakespeare, the first literary dictator and poet-laureate, and the man who most strongly shaped English letters after him. Jonson came of Annandale stock over the Solway, the same ground that later gave the world Thomas Carlyle.

The introduction follows his hard start. His father lost his estate under Queen Mary, was cast into prison, entered the church, and died a month before his son was born at Westminster early in 1573. The widow married a bricklayer, and the boy was apprenticed to that trade. Then the antiquary William Camden, an usher at Westminster School, took notice of him, and there Jonson laid the solid ground of his classical learning. The fox play that follows shows what that learning built.
